implementation_notes: JDK 9 put the pattern's interfaces into java.base: Publisher.subscribe registers a Subscriber, onSubscribe delivers a Subscription through which the subscriber requests items (the backpressure mechanism), and SubmissionPublisher is a ready-made broadcast channel that fans out to all current subscribers with an executor. The interfaces correspond one-to-one to the reactive-streams specification, so implementations interoperate across libraries. For plain in-application events where backpressure is irrelevant, a listener list or a framework facility is lighter, but Flow is the standard, dependency-free channel.
pitfalls: A Subscriber that never calls Subscription.request() receives nothing; a silent consumer is usually a missing request, not a broken publisher.
submit() blocks when the publisher's buffer is full; use offer(item, timeout, unit) or configure onDrop/maxBufferCapacity for a hot channel.
Subscriber methods for one subscription are strictly ordered, but no locking is provided around the subscriber's own state across subscriptions.

variants.name: Spring application events (ApplicationEventPublisher)
variants.implementation_notes: In a Spring application the container is the event channel: publishEvent hands the event to the ApplicationEventMulticaster, which invokes every matching ApplicationListener or @EventListener bean, optionally asynchronously and with transaction-phase binding. Publishers depend on one framework interface and consumers register by annotation, so there is no subscription bookkeeping at all; @TransactionalEventListener even delays delivery until the publishing transaction commits. Use it inside Spring applications, and keep Flow or a plain listener list where the framework must not be involved.
pitfalls: By default listeners run synchronously on the publisher's thread and inside its transaction: a listener exception propagates back to the publisher.
publishEvent is a hand-off with no ordering or delivery guarantee, and @Async listeners lose thread-bound context such as the current security principal.
Listener bean types are matched structurally - an event class hierarchy silently fans out to more listeners than intended.
